nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the populist dystopia and the crank prophecy
literary_identity: Politician, novelist and crank; the author of Caesar's Column, the great American dystopia of the 1890s.
biography: Born Ignatius Loyola Donnelly in Philadelphia on 3 November 1831; he moved to Minnesota, was lieutenant-governor and a congressman, and led the Populist Party in the state. Caesar's Column (1890), Atlantis (1882) and The Great Cryptogram (1888) followed. He died in Minneapolis on 1 January 1901.
literary_profile: Donnelly wrote Caesar's Column, the great American dystopia of the 1890s and the forerunner of the twentieth-century anti-utopia: its vision of the class war and the coming tyranny made it a bestseller and a central text of American populism, and it is the direct ancestor of Orwell's and Huxley's nightmares.
stylistic_characteristics: The future history narrated from a later age; the journey through the ruined city; the monstrous machine of the execution; the documentary statistics of inequality; the prophetic denunciation.
intellectual_concerns: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital.
historical_significance: Ignatius Donnelly wrote Caesar's Column, the great American dystopia of the 1890s and the forerunner of the anti-utopia: its vision of class war and tyranny made it a populist bestseller and the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century dystopian novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the single tax and the political economy of poverty
literary_identity: Political economist and journalist; the author of Progress and Poverty, the most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in Philadelphia on 2 September 1839; he went to sea, settled in California, and worked as a printer and journalist. Progress and Poverty (1879) sold in millions and made him a world figure; he ran for mayor of New York in 1886 and 1897, and died during the second campaign on 29 October 1897.
literary_profile: Henry George wrote the most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century: Progress and Poverty made the single tax a world movement, was translated into every major language, and shaped the progressive and labour politics of Britain, America and Australia for a generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, forceful argument addressed to the common reader; the paradox stated and pursued; the historical survey of wages and rent; the moral appeal against the injustice of the land; the reformer's directness.
intellectual_concerns: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment.
historical_significance: Henry George wrote the most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century: Progress and Poverty made the single tax a world movement and shaped progressive and labour politics in Britain, America and Australia for a generation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the realist of the small town and the clerical crisis
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of The Damnation of Theron Ware, one of the finest American novels of the 1890s.
biography: Born Harold Henry Frederick in Utica, New York, on 14 August 1856; he worked on the Utica Observer and the Albany Evening Journal and became the London correspondent of the New York Times in 1884. Seth's Brother's Wife (1887), The Lawton Girl (1890), The Damnation of Theron Ware (1896) and ill-fated Gloria Mundi (1898) followed. He died in London on 19 October 1898.
literary_profile: Harold Frederic wrote The Damnation of Theron Ware, one of the finest American novels of the 1890s and the first American novel to treat the crisis of a clergyman's faith with full intellectual seriousness: it anticipates the modern novel of belief and the naturalist study of the small town.
stylistic_characteristics: The free indirect style of the provincial mind; the small-town detail and the church social; the intellectual temptation and the sexual one; the irony of the convert; the documentary accuracy of the Methodist parsonage.
intellectual_concerns: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil.
historical_significance: Harold Frederic wrote The Damnation of Theron Ware, one of the finest American novels of the 1890s and the first American novel to treat a clergyman's crisis of faith with full intellectual seriousness: it is a direct ancestor of the modern novel of belief and of the naturalist small-town novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the heroic revival and the Ulster cycle
literary_identity: Historian, journalist and novelist; the writer who reintroduced the Irish heroic sagas to the nineteenth century and inspired the Irish Literary Revival.
biography: Born at Castletown Berehaven, County Cork, on 18 September 1846; he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and practised law before History of Ireland: Heroic Period (1878) made him the herald of the Irish revival. Cuculain and His Contemporaries (1880), The Story of Ireland (1894) and The Bog of Stars (1893) followed. He died on the Isle of Wight on 18 May 1928.
literary_profile: Standish O'Grady was the writer who reintroduced the Irish heroic sagas to the nineteenth century and the man Yeats called the father of the Irish Literary Revival: his History of Ireland and his Cuculain books made the Ulster cycle available to modern literature and gave the revival its heroic subject.
stylistic_characteristics: The retelling of the saga in Victorian prose; the heroic epithet and the set speech; the landscape of the Irish epic; the historian's narrative frame; the romantic nationalism of the address.
intellectual_concerns: National identity and the heroic code; the Irish past and the recovery of the native tradition; heroism and the warrior elite; the relation of the poet to the nation; the Celtic periphery.
historical_significance: Standish James O'Grady reintroduced the Irish heroic sagas to the nineteenth century and was called by Yeats the father of the Irish Literary Revival: his History of Ireland and his Cuculain books made the Ulster cycle available to modern literature and gave the revival its heroic subject.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Galway novel and the Irish historical lyric
literary_identity: Novelist, historian and poet; the finest woman novelist of the Irish revival and the author of Hurrish and Grania.
biography: Born the Hon. Emily Lawless at Lyons, County Kildare, on 17 June 1845, the daughter of the third Baron Cloncurry; she grew up in Kildare and in the Burren of County Clare. Hurrish (1886), Grania (1892), Maelcho (1894) and the poems With the Wild Geese (1902) followed. She died at Gomshall, Surrey, on 2 December 1913.
literary_profile: Emily Lawless was the finest woman novelist of the Irish revival: Hurrish and Grania brought the west of Ireland and the Aran Islands into fiction with a realism that neither the Celtic Twilight nor the peasant play could match, and With the Wild Geese is one of the great Irish historical poem sequences.
stylistic_characteristics: The western landscape as the determining force; the Aran and Burren detail; the heroine divided between two men and two Irelands; the historical retrospect of the Jacobite wars; the plain, unsentimental prose.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; the countryside, the vanishing rural world; the woman question and the limited estate; the Celtic periphery and the imperial centre; national identity and the heroic past.
historical_significance: Emily Lawless was the finest woman novelist of the Irish revival: Hurrish and Grania brought the west of Ireland and the Aran Islands into fiction with a realism the Celtic Twilight could not match, and With the Wild Geese is one of the great Irish historical poem sequences.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Irish lyric and the London man of letters
literary_identity: Poet and diarist; the author of 'The Fairies' and one of the finest Irish lyric poets of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in Ballyshannon, County Donegal, on 12 March 1824; he worked in the customs service in Ireland and England, published Poems (1850) and Day and Night Songs (1854), and edited Fraser's Magazine from 1874. Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland (1864) is his long Irish poem, and his diary records the London of Tennyson, Carlyle and Rossetti. He died in Hampstead on 18 November 1889.
literary_profile: William Allingham wrote the finest Irish lyric of the mid-nineteenth century and one of the best diaries in the language: 'The Fairies' is the most anthologised Irish poem of the century, Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland is the first sustained Irish social poem, and his diary is a central record of Victorian literary London.
stylistic_characteristics: The short lyric of the fairy world; the ballad refrain of the Irish tradition; the long poem of Irish rural society; the diary as literary form; the plain, musical, unornamented line.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; the countryside, the vanishing rural world; the superstition and the fairy faith; poverty and the landlord's Ireland; the metropolis and the literary marketplace.
historical_significance: William Allingham wrote the finest Irish lyric of the mid-nineteenth century and one of the best literary diaries in the language: 'The Fairies' is the most anthologised Irish poem of the century, and Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland is the first sustained Irish social poem.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the novel of the woman's vocation
literary_identity: Novelist, reviewer and correspondent; the author of The Half Sisters and one of the most influential literary women of the mid-Victorian period.
biography: Born Geraldine Endsor Jewsbury at Measham, Derbyshire, on 22 August 1812; she moved to Manchester and then London, where she became the reader for Bentley's and a reviewer for the Athenaeum, and the intimate friend of Jane Welsh Carlyle. Zoe (1845), The Half Sisters (1848), Marian Withers (1851) and Constance Herbert (1855) followed. She died in London on 23 September 1880.
literary_profile: Geraldine Jewsbury wrote The Half Sisters, one of the most important English novels of the woman's vocation and a founding text of the novel of female independence: her Manchester setting, her professional heroine and her argument that a woman's work is her life made her the most radical of the pre-Braddon novelists and a model for the New Woman fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The double heroine divided between marriage and vocation; the Manchester commercial setting; the argument in dialogue; the reviewer's irony; the refusal of the conventional ending.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.
historical_significance: Geraldine Jewsbury wrote The Half Sisters, one of the most important English novels of the woman's vocation: her Manchester setting, her professional heroine and her argument that a woman's work is her life made her the most radical of the pre-Braddon novelists and a direct model for New Woman fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Dorset dialect poet and the philologist
literary_identity: Poet, philologist and clergyman; the finest English dialect poet of the nineteenth century and the author of Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect.
biography: Born at Rushay in the parish of Bagber, Dorset, on 22 February 1801; he kept a school in Dorchester, was ordained in 1847, and served as curate and then rector at Winterborne Came. Poems in the Dorset Dialect (1844), Hwomely Rhymes (1859) and Poems of Rural Life in Common English (1868) followed, with his philological works on English grammar and etymology. He died at Winterborne Came on 7 October 1886.
literary_profile: William Barnes was the finest English dialect poet of the nineteenth century and one of the great English philologists: his Dorset poems are the most complete record of the English rural world in its own speech, and his campaign against the Latinisation of English grammar made him a pioneer of the study of the vernacular.
stylistic_characteristics: The Dorset dialect in its full grammar; the eclogue and the rural dialogue; the catalogue of the farm and the workshop; the elegy for the vanished custom; the plain, monosyllabic, pre-Latinate diction.
intellectual_concerns: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; the labour of the farm and the craftsman; the dialect and the local community; education and the rural school; the memory of the dead.
historical_significance: William Barnes was the finest English dialect poet of the nineteenth century: his Dorset poems are the most complete record of the English rural world in its own speech, his philology made him a pioneer of vernacular studies, and both Hardy and Hopkins admired him as a master.
